title: Forms, words, and decision-friendly defaults
outcome: Write labels, hints, validation, and empty states that help users act correctly.
useCase: Operational forms and bulk actions with meaningful consequences.
benefits: Reduces confusion without adding long tutorials.
drawbacks: Concise language still needs domain accuracy and localization.
version: Web UX · WCAG 2.2 · principles, not magic formulas
cue: Label the value. Explain the rule. Name the next action.

trace.title: Task language
trace.detail:
## Understand the idea

Words are interface controls.

“Submit” may be less clear than “Assign 15 tickets.” A label names the input; a hint explains a constraint; an error explains what is wrong and how to repair it.

Placeholder text is not a stable replacement for a label.

Ask only for information needed now. Explain unusual requirements before users fail.

Choose defaults from the task and make their scope visible. A default workspace or audience can create a serious mistake if it is hidden.

Empty, loading, no-results, and failed are different states.

“No tickets yet” is not the same as “No tickets match these filters” or “We could not load tickets.” Each needs a different next action.

trace.title: Follow one item
trace.detail:
Read the task → understand the field → enter a value → see timely validation → repair if needed → confirm the result.

Check whether people understand the terms without internal team knowledge.

For defaults, test changing workspace, returning later, and repeating the action. A remembered choice can become wrong when context changes.

trace.title: Try the failure
trace.detail:
Required markers without an explanation can be confusing. A disabled button without a reason hides progress.

Internal error codes tell users little about the repair.

recallPrompt: Without notes: Write labels, hints, validation, and empty states that help users act correctly. Explain one example and one failure.
